meta.title: Security and Quality Audit
meta.app: Chairside - salon and barbershop booking app
meta.subtitle: Findings, business impact, and remediation
meta.confidentiality: Confidential - prepared for the application owner

executiveSummary.intro: This report reviews a salon and barbershop booking app for security and correctness, and documents the fixes applied. It is written for the business owner: each finding explains what was found, why it matters for the business, and what was done about it.
executiveSummary.foundationNote: The app is built on solid foundations. The database keeps each salon's data separate, visitors cannot read the tables directly, and the system already prevents two bookings landing on the same person at the same time. The automated security scan offered by the build platform reported no issues at the time of the audit (October 2026); that same report notes it cannot catch every possible risk.
executiveSummary.theme: The issues found are subtler than missing basics: the booking and permission rules were enforced only in the app's screens, not on the server. Anyone who talks to the system directly, bypassing the screens, could do things the screens never allow. That is the thread running through the most serious findings.
executiveSummary.outcome: Of 19 findings, the 2 High and most Medium issues are fixed or materially reduced; the rest are documented with clear recommendations. Fixes were made so that each one is backed by an automated test. The original app is preserved unchanged for before-and-after comparison.
executiveSummary.testRun: Latest test run (2026-10-12): 42 tests, 41 passed, 1 skipped (an environment-dependent time-zone demonstration).
topRisks: A stranger who knew a client's phone number could change that client's name and email.
Bookings could be created at closed times (03:00, closed days, or years ahead) by bypassing the app.
Any staff member could delete a client and that client's entire history.
A single visitor could flood the calendar with fake bookings.
Typing someone's email into the staff list could silently give them access to your client data.

strengths: Each salon's data is isolated from every other salon's (verified by tests).
Anonymous visitors cannot read database tables directly; public actions go only through a small set of controlled functions.
Double-booking the same staff member at the same time is prevented by the database itself.
Prices on past bookings are snapshotted, so later price changes do not rewrite history.
The powerful server key never reaches the browser.
The AI features run as the signed-in user, so they cannot reach another salon's clients.

findings.title: A visitor could change an existing client's name and email
findings.found: The public booking flow identified clients by phone number. A booking made with an existing client's phone number overwrote that client's stored name and email with whatever was typed.
findings.impact: Anyone who knew (or guessed) a client's phone number could rename that client and change their email, and the new booking attached to that client's history and notes. This corrupts the client list and could be used to impersonate or harass a client.
findings.fix: The booking flow no longer overwrites an existing client's name or email. The name entered at booking time is now stored separately and shown to staff when it differs from the client on file, so staff can verify it is the same person. Fully preventing a stranger from attaching to a known phone number requires a phone verification step (a one-time code) at booking, which is recommended as a next step.

findings.title: Bookings could be made at impossible times
findings.found: The rules about opening hours, open days and how far ahead clients may book existed only in the app's screens. Calling the booking service directly, the only server check was that the time was not in the past.
findings.impact: Someone bypassing the app could create appointments while the salon is closed, outside opening hours, or years in the future. The calendar stops reflecting reality and staff cannot trust it.
findings.fix: The server now enforces the salon's open days, opening hours, a 21-day booking window, and valid time slots - all evaluated in the salon's own time zone.

findings.title: Staff could do more than their role should allow
findings.found: Any staff member could edit and delete client records, and could read every booking in the salon. Deleting a client also deleted that client's entire booking and note history.
findings.impact: A single stylist could wipe a client's whole history, or browse other staff members' clients - well beyond 'see your own calendar'.
findings.fix: Staff can now read clients (needed to keep notes) but only the owner can change or delete them. Each staff member now sees only their own appointments; the owner still sees all.

findings.title: No limit on public bookings
findings.found: A single anonymous visitor could create an unlimited number of bookings; there was no rate limit or quota.
findings.impact: An attacker could fill the calendar and client table with fake entries and make the system unusable for the salon.
findings.fix: The server now limits how many upcoming bookings a single phone number can hold and how many bookings a salon accepts in a short window. Network-level rate limiting per visitor and a CAPTCHA are recommended as an additional layer, along with a usage limit on the AI features.

findings.title: Staff invitations joined people without consent
findings.found: Adding an email address to the staff list silently linked that person to the salon the next time they signed in, with no acceptance step.
findings.impact: A person could be given access to a salon's client data without ever agreeing to join, and the behaviour was unpredictable when an email belonged to more than one salon.
findings.fix: Invitations now require explicit acceptance: the invited person sees a pending invitation and must click Accept, and only an invitation addressed to their own email can be accepted.

findings.title: No limits on booking form input
findings.found: The booking form accepted names, phone numbers and emails of unlimited length and with no format checking (a 20,000-character name was accepted).
findings.impact: Oversized or malformed data could break staff screens and outgoing messages and bloat the database.
findings.fix: The server now checks the length and basic format of the name, phone number and email.

findings.title: Missing security headers
findings.found: The app sent none of the standard browser security headers (such as a content security policy or anti-framing header).
findings.impact: The site could be embedded invisibly in a malicious page to trick clients (clickjacking), and browser defences against injected scripts were weaker than they should be.
findings.fix: Every response now carries a content security policy and the other standard security headers. The policy was verified against the running app so it protects without breaking any feature.

findings.title: Login session stored in the browser
findings.found: The login session token is kept in the browser's local storage.
findings.impact: If a script-injection flaw ever occurred, an attacker could read the session and take over the account.
findings.fix: Recommended: store the session in a secure, script-inaccessible cookie. The content security policy added above reduces the risk in the meantime.

findings.title: Personal data handling and the AI features
findings.found: Client personal data (name, phone, email, notes, visit history) is sent to an outside AI provider for the summary and reminder features. There was no stated retention period, no deletion or export path, and no privacy notice on the booking page.
findings.impact: Clients' personal data leaves the salon's system with no stated handling, and the salon cannot easily honour a request to delete someone's data.
findings.fix: A short privacy notice was added to the booking page. Recommended: minimise what is sent to the AI, define a retention period with automatic deletion, and add a way to export or erase a client's data on request.

findings.title: Business rules lived only in the app screens
findings.found: Opening hours, the booking window, cancel and move rules and revenue all lived in the browser, not on the server.
findings.impact: Anyone bypassing the app screens could ignore the salon's rules.
findings.fix: The booking rules were moved onto the server and into the database access rules (see BH-01 and SEC-03).

findings.title: Time slots used the visitor's time zone
findings.found: The list of free time slots was calculated using the visitor's device time zone, while the salon's opening hours are stored without a time zone.
findings.impact: A client in another region saw shifted times and could book a slot that is not actually open at the salon; two clients in different regions picking the same time sent two different real times.
findings.fix: Slots are now computed in the salon's own time zone, so every visitor sees the same real opening times.

findings.title: Lists and dashboard will under-report at scale
findings.found: Lists and the dashboard have no paging and silently stop at the first 1000 rows; revenue is added up in the browser.
findings.impact: As the salon grows, the dashboard and lists will quietly show incomplete or wrong totals.
findings.fix: Recommended: calculate totals and popular services on the server and add paging to the lists.

findings.title: Data model: phone duplicates and no audit trail
findings.found: Clients are identified by phone number with no normalisation (so '+90...', '0...' and spaced variants could create duplicates), deletes cascade, and there is no record of who changed what.
findings.impact: The same client entered two ways becomes two records, and deletions remove history with no audit trail.
findings.fix: Phone numbers are now normalised to one format before saving, and uniqueness is enforced on the normalised value. Recommended: soft-delete (hide rather than erase) and an audit trail.

findings.title: Booking-link not cleaned on the server
findings.found: A salon's public booking-link (slug) was not sanitised when set directly through the service, bypassing the app's cleanup.
findings.impact: Broken or confusing public booking links.
findings.fix: The server now normalises the booking-link and enforces a safe format; it also now rejects negative prices.

findings.title: AI reminder could be steered by note content
findings.found: Client name and notes flow directly into the AI prompt, and the AI-written reminder is sent from the salon's own phone number.
findings.impact: Someone could try to steer the reminder message (for example to insert a link) by writing instructions into a client's note or name.
findings.fix: Untrusted text is now clearly marked as data rather than instructions, and links are stripped from the reminder before it can be sent. A working exploit was not reproduced; this hardens the design.

findings.title: Environment file in the repository; dependency advisories
findings.found: An environment file was committed to the generated project (it contained only the public key), and there are development-only dependency advisories.
findings.impact: Low: the committed key is public by design, and the advisories affect only the development tools, not the live app.
findings.fix: Recommended: keep environment files out of the repository and update the affected development tool.

findings.title: Password-guessing was not rate-limited (test project)
findings.found: Password strength, email confirmation and protection against revealing which emails are registered were all in good shape. However, repeated wrong-password attempts were not throttled in the test project.
findings.impact: Without a limit, automated password-guessing against an account is easier.
findings.fix: Recommended: confirm the production setting and enable rate limiting or temporary lockout after repeated failures.

findings.title: Thin automated tests; some loosely-typed code
findings.found: The generated app shipped with a single automated test and some loosely-typed code.
findings.impact: Lower confidence that future changes will not quietly break something.
findings.fix: Recommended: broaden automated test coverage and tighten types. This audit adds a runnable security test suite as a starting point.

findings.title: Internal helper functions callable by anyone
findings.found: Two internal helper functions could be called by anonymous visitors (harmless: they return nothing useful to an anonymous caller).
findings.impact: No practical impact; addressed as defence in depth.
findings.fix: Access to the helper functions is now restricted to signed-in users.

hardening: Anonymous visitors had database-level table privileges by default, leaving the access rules as the only line of defence; those privileges were removed, so anonymous visitors can now use only the controlled public functions.
Phone numbers are normalised to one format so the same client is not stored twice.

roadmap.item: Move the login session to a secure, script-inaccessible cookie
Server-side totals and paging for lists and the dashboard
Data retention, deletion and export; minimise data sent to the AI
Per-visitor rate limiting and a CAPTCHA at the edge; AI usage limit
Confirm production auth settings and enable password-guessing protection
Keep environment files out of the repository; update development tools
Broaden automated tests; tighten types; soft-delete and audit trail

scope: Testing was limited to a locally running copy of the app and a separate test project with the same database structure applied to it. No hosted or production environment was accessed. All test data is fictitious.

reproduce.intro: The findings are backed by an automated test suite. To re-run it against your own test project, provide connection details in a local environment file (not included in this report) with these variable names:
envVars: AUDIT_GEMINI_API_KEY (only for the AI prompt-injection test)
steps: Run the test suite. With only the original structure applied, the finding tests fail (proving the issue); with the hardening applied, they pass (proving the fix).
